Question: What do the symbols in William Blake's "The Tyger" represent?
Answer: SYMBOLS IN WILLIAM BLAKE’S “THE TYGER” by Michael R. Burch William Blake’s poem “The Tyger” is laden with symbols and yet is the most anthologized poem in the English language. “The Tyger” has thus been perused and enjoyed by hundreds of millions, if not billions, of readers since it was first published in 1794. How laden with symbols? As I will demonstrate in my analysis, every line of “The Tyger” contains a symbol, and some lines contain multiple symbols. However, these symbols are accessible and easily understood. “The Tyger” is an easy poem to understand, if we connect the dots. However, the majority of readers have failed to connect the dots and thus have entirely missed the poem’s main point, which is wildly heretical and casts extreme doubt on the nature and intentions of God, as I will explain in my analysis of “The Tyger” below. But first, who was William Blake? William Blake was an English poet, painter, engraver and mystic who included “The Tyger” in his 1794 collection Songs of Experience. Ironically, Blake had to self-publish his books because he was considered mad and his poetry of little account. However, readers of the future would judge otherwise and today William Blake is widely acclaimed as one of the world’s greatest and most influential poets. Elsewhere, I have argued that Blake is the world’s most influential poet in terms of his impact on human societies and culture, due to his anti-establishment, reform-minded influence on wildly popular singer-songwriters like Bob Dylan, John Lennon, Jim Morrison, et al. Morrison named his band The Doors after Blake’s “doors of perception.” When the Beatles met Bob Dylan the first time, things were a bit chilly until Allen Ginsberg broke the ice by bringing up the subject of William Blake’s poetry. It turned out that both Dylan and the Fab Four were enthusiastic fans of Blake. Blake has also had tremendous influence on other poets, visual artists, novelists, graphic novelists, cartoonists and filmmakers. And now, without further ado, this is my analysis of “The Tyger” including the poem’s various symbols and “how to connect the dots”… The Tyger by William Blake Tyger Tyger, burning bright, [1] In the forests of the night; [2] What immortal hand or eye, [3] Could frame thy fearful symmetry? [4] [1] Things that are bright are notable and attract our attention. The tiger is a magnificent, stunningly beautiful creature. [2] Forests symbolize nature and like the tiger are both beautiful and dangerous. The night symbolizes darkness, danger and things that are hidden, unseen and mysterious. [3] The “immortal hand” symbolizes the artistry and handiwork of the Creator. Artists like Blake create with their hands. Meanwhile, artists use their eyes to regard and judge their work. The Bible claims God saw his creation, and that in his eyes it was good. Those of us who see a world full of cruelty, suffering and death might argue otherwise, as Blake will in his most famous poem. [4] Here I believe “fearful symmetry” symbolizes seeming perfection in the merger of opposites: in the tiger’s case, extreme beauty with extreme deadliness and cruelty. The tiger is a beautiful but savage predator. Here, we see Blake subtly questioning the nature and intentions of the Creator, but he will be more explicit later. In what distant deeps or skies [5] Burnt the fire of thine eyes? [6] On what wings dare he aspire? [7] What the hand, dare seize the fire? [8] [5] In the opening verses of Genesis, the Creator created the depths [seas] and skies [the visible sky and the heavens above]. The modifier “distant” suggests things beyond the ability of human beings to see or understand. Thus the deeps may symbolize hell and the skies heaven. A critical question in Blake’s poem will be why the Creator fashioned the planet earth as he did, and what his intentions for human beings are. [6] Here fire symbolizes heat, passion, anger and destruction. Fire is also associated with hell and damnation. The Bible refers to a “lake of fire” and its place was said to be deep below the earth. If we combine lines five and six, Blake might be asking whether the tiger was created in heaven or hell. [7] Gods and angels have often been depicted with wings, which thus symbolize both divinity and abilities beyond those of human beings: to fly, to enter heaven, etc. To aspire is to intend and thus symbolizes what Christians call the “divine plan” but which Blake severely doubts, as we will see. [8] Here the hand seizing the fire symbolizes the Gnostic idea that the Creator was “in over his head” and that nothing good would come of his creation. According to gnostic theology, the Creator was evil, not good, and this explains why we live in a world ruled by cruelty, suffering and death. Hands that seize fire get burned, so Blake may be prophesying that the Creator will have to pay for his misdeeds. And what shoulder, & what art, [9] Could twist the sinews of thy heart? [10] And when thy heart began to beat. [11] What dread hand? & what dread feet? [12] [9] Here the art is the method of the art of creation. Was it a dark art? I believe Blake thought so. Sculptors use their shoulders as well as their hands, and here shoulders suggest strength and heavy lifting. [10] Sinews also symbolize strength. The heart symbolizes courage. The tiger is wonderfully courageous and has a mighty heart, but how is that mighty heart employed? [11] The heart beginning to beat symbolizes the moment of birth, of creation. But what happens when that mighty heart begins to beat? Savagery, destruction, death. [12] The dread hand and dread feet are those of the Creator. Is the Creator even more savage and dreadful than his fearsome creation, the tiger? What the hammer? what the chain, [13] In what furnace was thy brain? [14] What the anvil? what dread grasp [15] Dare its deadly terrors clasp? [16] [13] The hammer symbolizes the creative powers of the Creator, but he is hammering out a chain on his anvil of creation. In another poem Blake railed against the “mind-forg’d manacles” that keep human beings slaves of church [bad religion] and state [bad government] and their own bad thinking. Here it seems this chaining, this enslavement, was part and parcel of creation. According to the Genesis creation account, Adam and Eve were created to be gardeners in an animal state, lacking the knowledge of good and evil. Was this the intention of the Creator? Blake seems to think so. [14] Here the furnace may symbolize hell. Was the tiger’s savage brain forged in hell rather than in heaven? [15] The anvil symbolizes where creation takes place. A blacksmith’s anvil is surrounded by fire, sparks and smoke. Is this a hellish anvil? Yes, it seems obviously so. The “dread grasp” echoes previous characteristics of the Creator. Is he more dreadful than his most dreadful creation, the tiger? [16] The “dread grasp” clasping “deadly terrors” again symbolizes and questions the nature of the Creator. What sort of Being is able to dominate the savage tiger while fashioning chains to enslave it? And what are this Being’s intentions for human beings? When the stars threw down their spears [17] And water'd heaven with their tears: [18] Did he smile his work to see? [19] Did he who made the Lamb make thee? [20] [17] To the ancients the stars were divine beings — gods, angels, great hunters and heroes of yore who had become immortal after death. Does the throwing down of spears symbolize acknowledgement that the Creator was the greatest of them all? Or did the other divine beings throw down their spears in disgust? [18] Here, the stars watering heaven with their tears strongly suggests the other divine beings were very unhappy with the Creator’s handiwork. Why? Because they understood what the creation of the tiger meant for all the other creatures, and for human beings. [19] The Bible says the Creator saw his work as good, hence this smile symbolizes the happiness of the Creator with his creation, and with the tiger, the ultimate predator. [20] Here the Lamb is capitalized, and this is no accident. The lamb symbolizes innocence and purity with its downy coat of white wool, vulnerability, sacrifice, and the person of Jesus Christ, who was called the Lamb of God. Furthermore, the Lamb capitalized refers to Blake’s poem “The Lamb” which appeared in Songs of Innocence and is a companion poem to “The Tyger.” When Blake asks, “Did he who made the Lamb make thee?” he is asking a freighted question for Christians and for everyone who claims that “God is good.” Blake is questioning the nature of a God who would create an innocent, defenseless lamb to be ripped to shreds and eaten by such a savage predator as the tiger. And he is questioning the nature of a God who would send his “only begotten son” to earth to be crucified as a bloody sacrifice. Elsewhere, Blake would call this alleged god NOBODADDY because no one would want him for a father. Tyger Tyger burning bright, In the forests of the night: What immortal hand or eye, Dare frame thy fearful symmetry? Blake ends his famous poem the way he began it, with the exception of the word “dare” in the concluding line. Is Blake asking, “How dare the Creator do what he did, and will he pay for his crimes against life?” At least that’s the way I interpret the poem. by Michael R. Burch #BLAKE #TYGER #MRBBLAKE #MRBTYGER

Question: Is Emerson as great a poet as Whitman and Baudelaire?
Answer: I would not rank Ralph Waldo Emerson in the same category as Walt Whitman and Charles Baudelaire as a poet. Emerson is better known as a philosopher and essayist than as a poet. This is probably Emerson’s best-known poem. It’s a reasonably good poem, but not a great poem and doesn’t approach the best poems of Whitman and Baudelaire in my opinion. Brahma by Ralph Waldo Emerson If the red slayer think he slays, Or if the slain think he is slain, They know not well the subtle ways I keep, and pass, and turn again. … Walt Whitman is arguably a top ten poet of all time and almost single-handedly created modern free verse, the dominant form of poetry today. Whitman’s masterpieces include “A Noiseless Patient Spider” (my personal favorite), “Song of Myself,” “I Sing the Body Electric,” “When I Heard the Learn'd Astronomer,” “Out of the Cradle Endlessly Rocking” and his elegies for Abraham Lincoln “When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom’d” and “O Captain! My Captain!” (his only famous rhyming poem). Charles Baudelaire was a marvelous French poet, not quite the stature of Whitman, but very highly regarded around the world. These are my translations of some of his poems. The first two have been “borrowed” by a number of adult websites and escort services! So the pros evidently like Baudelaire. Le Balcon (The Balcony) by Charles Baudelaire, a French poet loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Paramour of memory, ultimate mistress, source of all pleasure, my only desire; how can I forget your ecstatic caresses, the warmth of your breasts by the roaring fire, paramour of memory, ultimate mistress? Each night illumined by the burning coals we lay together where the rose-fragrance clings— how soft your breasts, how tender your soul! Ah, and we said imperishable things, each night illumined by the burning coals. How beautiful the sunsets these sultry days, deep space so profound, beyond life's brief floods ... then, when I kissed you, my queen, in a daze, I thought I breathed the bouquet of your blood as beautiful as sunsets these sultry days. Night thickens around us like a wall; in the deepening darkness our irises meet. I drink your breath, ah! poisonous yet sweet!, as with fraternal hands I massage your feet while night thickens around us like a wall. I have mastered the sweet but difficult art of happiness here, with my head in your lap, finding pure joy in your body, your heart; because you're the queen of my present and past I have mastered love's sweet but difficult art. O vows! O perfumes! O infinite kisses! Can these be reborn from a gulf we can't sound as suns reappear, as if heaven misses their light when they sink into seas dark, profound? O vows! O perfumes! O infinite kisses! Les Bijoux (The Jewels) by Charles Baudelaire loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch My lover nude and knowing my heart's whims Wore nothing more than a few bright-flashing gems; Her art was saving men despite their sins— She ruled like harem girls crowned with diadems! She danced for me with a gay but mocking air, My world of stone and metal sparking bright; I discovered in her the rapture of everything fair— Nay, an excess of joy where the spirit and flesh unite! Naked she lay and offered herself to me, Parting her legs and smiling receptively, As gentle and yet profound as the rising sea— Till her surging tide encountered my cliff, abruptly. A tigress tamed, her eyes met mine, intent ... Intent on lust, content to purr and please! Her breath, both languid and lascivious, lent An odd charm to her metamorphoses. Her limbs, her loins, her abdomen, her thighs, Oiled alabaster, sinuous as a swan, Writhed pale before my calm clairvoyant eyes; Like clustered grapes her breasts and belly shone. Skilled in more spells than evil imps can muster, To break the peace which had possessed my heart, She flashed her crystal rocks’ hypnotic luster Till my quietude was shattered, blown apart. Her waist awrithe, her breasts enormously Out-thrust, and yet ... and yet, somehow, still coy ... As if stout haunches of Antiope Had been grafted to a boy ... The room grew dark, the lamp had flickered out. Mute firelight, alone, lit each glowing stud; Each time the fire sighed, as if in doubt, It steeped her pale, rouged flesh in pools of blood. Question: Is William Wordsworth out of fashion? Far less people seem to care about him than Blake nowadays.
Answer: Both William Blake and William Wordsworth remain influential today, albeit in different ways. William Blake has had the greater influence on modern thinking and culture: for instance, through his anti-establishment, reform-minded, free-thinking influence on singer-songwriters like Bob Dylan, John Lennon and Jim Morrison of the Doors. The Doors were named after Blake’s “doors of perception.” When Dylan met the Beatles for the first time and things were a bit icy at first, the poet Allen Ginsberg broke the ice by bringing up William Blake. It turned out that both Dylan and the Beatles were enthusiastic fans of Blake. William Wordsworth has had the greater influence on how poetry is written. His elegant blank verse has been a touchstone for many poets who followed him. Notable poets influenced by Wordsworth include his friend and sometimes partner Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Percy Bysshe Shelley (esp. “The Sunset,” “Alastor,” “Hymn to Intellectual Beauty” and “Mont Blanc”), John Keats (esp. “I stood tip-toe upon a little hill” and "Sleep and Poetry"), Lord Byron (less so, but in spots), Alfred Tennyson (in spots, esp. “Dora”), Walt Whitman (like Wordsworth a pantheist), Matthew Arnold (in spots, esp. “The Hayswater Boat”), Robert Frost (blank verse), Hart Crane (blank verse), Wallace Stevens (blank verse) and Elizabeth Bishop. Wordsworth also resurrected the sonnet, which had fallen into neglect, and thus influenced notable penners of sonnets such as Keats, Shelley, Tennyson, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, Elizabeth Barrett Browning, Christina Rossetti, Edgar Allan Poe, Gerard Manley Hopkins, Edna St. Vincent Millay and e. e. cummings. Wordsworth continues to influence writers, even if they don’t recognize his influence, via his ideas about writing poetry that he and Coleridge jointly expressed in the preface to Lyrical Ballads. These ideas include the communication of emotion recollected in tranquility; using the actual language being spoken rather than a highly ornate art-ificial (if you’ll pardon the pun) language; and dealing with the real world, common things and commoners, rather than kings, lords and heroes of yore.

Question: People who were around in 1974, who did you pick to win Ali vs Foreman?
Answer: Nearly everyone picked George Foreman to defeat Muhammad Ali in the infamous “Rumble in the Jungle”. And there were widespread fears that the fearsome Foreman would seriously injure the aging and seemingly washed-up Ali. The 1974 fight was hardly seen as a clash of ring Titans. Foreman and his camp were all smiles before the overhyped “rumble,” confident of victory. An easy victory, like 40 others. On the other hand Ali was 32 and had lost the fabulous speed that had once set him apart from other heavyweights. Furthermore, the older, slower, underpowered Ali had lost to two boxers Foreman had demolished via second-round knockouts: Joe Frazier and Ken Norton. When Ali managed to come back and win the rematches, it was by the skin of his teeth. There simply was no comparison between the much younger, in-his-prime, more powerful Foreman and the much diminished Ali. With the benefit of perfect hindsight, we forget how far Ali had fallen from grace in the eyes of the boxing world. Ali’s heyday had ended seven years prior — an eternity in boxing years. Ali had dominated the heavyweight division from 1964 to 1967, but that was ancient history. What had he done for boxing fans lately, other than lose to and eke out narrow victories over his best opponents? After fighting the diminished Ali in 1970, when he was three years past his prime, Jerry Quarry said: “He’s still damn good, but he ain’t what he was. If you want to see Ali when he was Ali, watch the Cleveland Williams fight. And the much-prophesied Stumble in the Jungle was seven years past Ali’s prime. Ali still talked a good fight, but the boxing world was not impressed and predicted consensus doom for the all-talk Louisville Lip. The only question was how long Ali could last before Foreman knocked him out. Could he make it past the second round, even? Almost no one associated with boxing, not even Ali's long-time friend and supporter Howard Cosell, gave the fast-fading former champion a plugged nickel’s chance of winning. Younger, more formidable boxers had failed to do so for three years prior to the 1974 mismatch! Foreman was a brooding and intimidating presence — a bigger, scarier Mike Tyson — who seemed invincible. He was 40-0 with a staggering 37 knockouts, please pardon the pun. He had a 92.5% knockout rate. No fighter had ever gone more than 10 rounds with Foreman, and only three of those. Fearsome Foreman had a string of 24 consecutive knockouts and in his previous 12 fights only one boxer had made it past the second round. Luis Faustino Pires managed to eke into the fourth round before getting destroyed. In those 12 fights, Foreman’s opponents averaged exactly 2.0 rounds per match. Foreman’s ability to knock out quality opponents so quickly was unprecedented in boxing history. Foreman was a juggernaut. And he was in his prime at age 25, seven years younger than Ali. Howard Cosell predicted doom for the underpowered, washed up Ali. So did professional oddsmakers. There were rumors that Ali’s camp feared for his health, perhaps even for his life. Ali put up a brave front, but nearly everyone thought it was all for show. He would collect a nice fat paycheck, then fade into obscurity, as past-their-prime heavyweights who hung on too long invariably do. At this stage of his career, Ali was more celebrity poet than a legitimate challenger to Foreman’s heavyweight belt, mantle and crown. All the charismatic Ali could do was charm the media and adoring Zaire crowds with amusing rhymes: "If you think the world was surprised when Nixon resigned, wait till I whup Foreman's behind!" "I've done something new for this fight. I done wrestled with an alligator, done tussled with a whale; handcuffed lightning, throw’d thunder in jail; only last week, I murdered a rock, injured a stone, hospitalized a brick; I'm so mean I make medicine sick." Of course Ali proved the world wrong and confirmed that he was, indeed, The Greatest, with a capital “T” and capital “G.” by Michael R. Question: What is the reason behind the catcher and shortstop positions in baseball being typically filled by weaker hitters?
Answer: Catcher and shortstop are baseball’s most demanding defensive positions and poor fielders and throwers at those positions will cost their teams runs. A player with a good bat and glove and strong arm who falls short of the range required for shortstop may end up at third base. A player with a good bat and glove but not-so-great arm may end up at second base. A player with a good bat and arm, but not-so-great infield glove, may end up in right field. A player who has a decent arm but not one strong enough for right field may end up in left field. A player with a good bat but limited range may end up at first base. A player who is poor at defense at any position may end up at DH. MLB teams try to get their best bats on the field where they will either help the defense or do the least damage. Catcher and shortstop are the most demanding defensive positions, so good hitting is a plus, but in general the average catcher and shortstop are not as good with the bat as the average players at other positions. by Michael R. Cush or Kush is associated with ancient Babylon, so Nimrod has also been associated with Babylon and the famous Tower of Babel. Nimrod is often portrayed as being black or swarthy in complexion. But these are, of course, artists’ imaginings. No one knows if Nimrod really existed, or what he looked like if he did. According to the Bible, Nimrod's kingdom included the cities of Babel/Babylon, Uruk/Erech, Akkad and Calneh, in Shinar, and he also built the Assyrian cities of Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, Calah and Resen: Cush was the father of Nimrod, who began to be a mighty one on the earth. From that land he went forth into Assyria, where he built Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, Calah, and Resen, which is between Nineveh and the great city of Calah. (Genesis 10:8-12) Nimrod is mentioned in Micah 5:6, which refers to Assyria as “the land of Nimrod,” and in 1 Chronicles 1:10, which includes Nimrod’s name in a genealogy. Nimrod’s prowess as a hunter was such that his skill became proverbial, and the ancients would compliment hunters by saying, “This man is like Nimrod, the greatest hunter in the world.” Nimrod has been associated with the Nephilim, a race of giants called “mighty men” in Genesis 6:4 (KJV). This association has led some to believe that Nimrod was a giant. Many legends sprang up around Nimrod. In Jewish legends, Nimrod was a polytheist who promoted the worship of many gods and thus was the sworn enemy of the monotheist Abraham, whom Nimrod tried to murder (Genesis Rabbah 38:13). Nimrod appears in the mythology of many ancient cultures, including Arabic, Armenian, Greek, Hungarian and Syrian. There is evidence that the Epic of Gilgamesh and the myths of Hercules may have had their origins in myths of Nimrod. However, in the Homilies (H 9:4-6), Nimrod is equated with Zoroaster. According to Wikipedia, the elusive Nimrod has not been attested in any non-biblical registers, records or king lists. Historians have failed to match Nimrod with any historically attested figure, or to find any historical, linguistic or genetic link between Mesopotamia and the kingdom of Kush, although one suggestion among Mesopotamian figures is Naram-Sin of Akkad, the grandson of the famous King Sargon the Great. He was the grandson of Ham, the son of Noah, a bold man, and of great strength of hand. He persuaded them not to ascribe it to God, as if it were through his means they were happy, but to believe that it was their own courage which procured that happiness. He also gradually changed the government into tyranny, seeing no other way of turning men from the fear of God, but to bring them into a constant dependence on his power. He also said he would be revenged on God, if He should have a mind to drown the world again; for that he would build a tower too high for the waters to reach. And that he would avenge himself on God for destroying their forefathers. Now the multitude were very ready to follow the determination of Nimrod, and to esteem it a piece of cowardice to submit to God; and they built a tower, neither sparing any pains, nor being in any degree negligent about the work: and, by reason of the multitude of hands employed in it, it grew very high, sooner than any one could expect; but the thickness of it was so great, and it was so strongly built, that thereby its great height seemed, upon the view, to be less than it really was. For it was Enheduanna who elevated Inanna above all the male gods of ancient Mesopotamia. Inanna was the Goddess of love, war, and fertility. Her title was “The Queen of Heaven” and she was also known as (or greatly influenced) Ishtar, Astarte and Aphrodite. Enheduanna may have been the first feminist, or at least the first feminist we know by name. In one of her poems Inanna kills An, the former chief deity in the Mesopotamian pantheon, and thus becomes the supreme leader of the gods. Did Enheduanna "promote" a female deity to the Queen of Heaven? Might this be considered the first feminist poem? Was Enheduanna countermanding the male-dominated society in which she lived, and perhaps even "projecting" her wishes on male rivals? Enheduanna was the daughter of the famous King Sargon the Great of Akkad. She is also the first ancient writer whose name remains known today. She appears to be the first named poet in human history and the first known author of prayers and hymns. Enheduanna, who lived circa 2285-2250 BCE, is also one of the first women we know by name. She was the entu (high priestess) of the goddess Inanna and the moon god Nanna (Sin) in the Sumerian city-state of Ur. Enheduanna's composition Nin-me-šara ("The Exaltation of Inanna"), which I have translated below, details her expulsion from Ur, located in southern Iraq, along with her prayerful request to the goddess for reinstatement. Enheduanna also composed 42 liturgical hymns addressed to temples across Sumer and Akkad. She was also the first editor of a poetry anthology, hymnal or songbook, and the first poet to write in the first person. Her Sumerian Temple Hymns was the first collection of its kind; indeed, Enheduanna so claimed in closing: "My king, something has been created that no one had created before." Question: How good was Kobe compared to other top 10 greats like Jordan, Lebron, Kareem, Wilt, Russell, Magic, Bird, Shaq, Hakeem, and Duncan? Do you think he is overrated or underrated?
Answer: KOBE BRYANT: THE GOOD, THE BAD & THE UGLY by Michael R. Burch Kobe Bryant’s best and worst career stats are separated into categories and analyzed below. I will make the case that Kobe is a top 20 player of all time, but not top 10 nor a GOAT candidate. This is where I rank Kobe, all-time: My All-Time NBA Top 25 (#1) Wilt Chamberlain: averaged 40 ppg/25 rpg in his prime (#2) Oscar Robertson: the original triple-double machine (#3) Michael Jordan: not as close to Wilt as many believe (#4) Jerry West: the LOGO with the three-pointer? OMG! (#5) Larry Bird: they called him Larry Legend for a reason (#6) Magic Johnson: they called him Magic for a reason (#7) Kareem Abdul-Jabbar: possessor of fabled sky hook (#8) LeBron James: still playing and still climbing (#9) Elgin Baylor: the prototype for Dr. J, MJ and Kobe (#10) Bob Pettit: the NBA's forgotten superstar (#11) Bill Russell: the all-time king if rings are the thing (#12) Charles Barkley: the Round Mound of Rebound (#13) Hakeem Olajuwon: Hakeem the Dream (#14) Julius Erving: forever known as Dr. J (#15) Rick Barry: a basketball genius, but unlikable (#16) Shaquille O'Neal: physically dominant but no Wilt (#17) Tim Duncan: the Big Fundamental (#18) David Robinson: the Admiral (#19) Kobe Bryant: the Black Mamba is analyzed below (#20) Stephen Curry: a slow start drops him a bit here (#21) John Stockton: the all-time leader in assists and steals (#22) Karl Malone: the Mailman always delivered (#23) Kevin McHale: a vastly underrated superstar (#24) Pistol Pete Maravich: the Pistol with the three-pointer? (#25) Walt Frazier: another vastly underrated superstar HIGH HONORABLE MENTION: Scottie Pippen, Chris Paul, George Mikan, Steve Nash, Kevin Durant, Bob Cousy, Kevin Garnett, John Havlicek, Dolph Schayes, Isiah Thomas, Clyde Drexler, Dirk Nowitzki KOBE BRYANT’S BEST CAREER STATS: THE GOOD 18 x All-Star, 12 x All-Defensive, 80.2 VORP (12th), 172.7 Win Shares (19th all-time, which is very good but not GOAT territory), 22.7 PER (29th, ditto), 4.55 BPM (31st), .1705 Win Shares per 48 Minutes (63rd, ditto), 25.0 points per game (14th), 5.2 rebounds per game, 4.7 assists per game, 1.4 steals per game, 83.7% free throw percentage, .382 FTr (he was better than average getting to the free throw line) Kobe Bryant was obviously a great basketball player, and I have him in my top 20 players of all time, but I think his fans tend to overrate Kobe’s strengths and discount his weaknesses. According to VORP, Win Shares, Win Shares/48, BPM and PER, players who rank with or above Kobe include stars not usually in GOAT discussions, such as Tim Duncan, David Robinson, Charles Barkley, Dirk Nowitzki, Chris Paul, Kevin Garnett, Clyde Drexler, John Stockton, Karl Malone, Reggie Miller, Julius Erving, Moses Malone, Oscar Robertson, Jerry West, Elgin Baylor and Bob Pettit. KOBE BRYANT’S BELOW-AVERAGE CAREER STATS: THE BAD Three point field goal percentage: 32.9% (not remotely close to the top 250 and well below the 35.5% average for Kobe’s era) Field goal percentage: 44.7% (not remotely close to the top 250 and slightly below the 45.1% average for Kobe’s era) FG+ (field goal percentage adjusted for era): 99 (slightly below league average) Effective field goal percentage: 48.2% (not remotely close to the top 250 and slightly below the 48.8% average for Kobe’s era) EFG+ (effective field goal percentage adjusted for era): 99 (slightly below league average) True shooting percentage: 55.0% (not in the top 250, although closer than the other shooting efficiency stats above; the league average TSP was 53.1% during Kobe’s career, so he was a bit better than the average Joe, but not good compared to the better volume scorers) Offensive rating: 110.4 (206th, in a tie with Nene and behind Derek Harper, Orlando Woolridge, Vern Fleming, Tom Owens and Lou Williams) FG Add: -298.7 (this is the number of points added or lost by field goal attempts above the league average; a point I have made elsewhere is that volume shooters who shoot below league norms are actually helping opponents when they shoot too much) Kobe Bryant’s below-average stats relate to offensive efficiency (or, more accurately, to offensive inefficiency). Kobe’s poor shot selection was perhaps his major weakness. Yes, Kobe made some seemingly-impossible shots — “hero shots” — but he missed a lot of ill-advised shots that reduced his overall offensive efficiency. Many basketball fans and some experts believe that if Kobe had passed to Shaq more, rather than taking so many “hero shots,” the Lakers could have won at least one more championship. Some may argue that Kobe was not below average compared to all NBA players, but as much as he shot, we must compare him to volume scorers. Unfortunately, Kobe is a lot closer to inefficient volume scorers like Allen Iverson and Russell Westbrook, than he is to highly efficient volume scorers like Steph Curry and Nikola Jokic. KOBE BRYANT’S WORST CAREER STATS: THE UGLY Turnovers: 4,010 (5th-worst all-time, and especially bad because Kobe is sandwiched between John Stockton and Jason Kidd, who handled the ball a lot more and had much higher assist/turnover ratios) Turnovers per game: 3.0 (8th-worst for players with 1,000 or more games) Triple-doubles: 21 (this is not a lot when six players have 100 or more, or five times as many triple-doubles) DBPM (defensive box plus/minus): -0.1 (not remotely close to the top 250) DRtg (defensive rating): 105.5 (not in the top 250) Has Kobe been overrated as a defender? Perhaps wildly overrated? The DBPM and DRtg stats seem to say so. Steal percentage: 2.07% (just 190th on the all-time list). While this is not “bad” for the average player, it’s surprising for a player with Kobe’s defensive rep. For instance, the much shorter and less athletic John Stockton averaged 3.46% and notable defensive guards like Michael Jordan, Chris Paul, Alvin Robertson and Maurice Cheeks are well above 3.00%. The really strange thing here is that steal percentage seems to be Kobe’s best individual defensive stat! But it came with a cost because as Kobe’s coach Phil Jackson pointed out in his book: “Kobe’s defense, to be accurate, has faltered in recent years, despite his presence on the league’s all-defensive team… Mesmerized by the ball, he’s gambled too frequently putting us out of position, forcing rotations that leave a man wide open, and doesn’t keep his feet on the ground.” What Phil Jackson and the defensive stats I cited seem to be telling us is that Kobe has been overrated as a defender, perhaps because he made so many impressive plays that people remember, while only his coach and the stats remember the times he gave opponents easy baskets by gambling and losing. And for all the chances he took, Kobe didn’t produce as many steals on a per-play basis as the better defensive guards. One analyst, whose name I was unable to determine, used the defensive component of RAPM to conclude that Kobe Bryant was “the most overrated defender imaginable.” While D-RAMP agreed that Kevin Garnett, Dwight Howard, Tim Duncan, Ron Artest, Chris Paul, Bruce Bowen and Tony Allen were superior defenders, year-after-year Kobe consistently appeared toward the bottom of the top 20 defenders. Someone commenting on the analysis opined: “I can’t remember the last time a player has coasted so long on reputation in annual awards. Bryant’s defensive highlights would be pretty good (he has been able to turn it on), but in terms of overall defensive impact over the course of a season? Meh.” (I will link to the very interesting analysis and discussion at the bottom of this page.) I am inclined to agree. I think Kobe was a visually exciting player, like Allen Iverson, who is remembered for the amazing things he did, while his miscues and inefficiencies are largely forgotten except by the stats. A major difference between Michael Jordan and Kobe Bryant was that MJ was both visually exciting and consistently efficient. None of the defensive stats seem to believe in Kobe. Nor did one of the greatest basketball coaches of all time. Food for thought, at least. IN-BETWEEN: THE GRAY AREA The following stats are not especially “good” or “bad” but fall somewhere in between. Rebounding percentage: 12.7% (good but not great for Kobe’s height) Blocks per game: 0.5 (not good for Kobe’s height and athleticism; John Stockton had the same stat) Block percentage: 1.0% (the average block percentage for a shooting guard is around 1.2%) TS+: 104 (true shooting adjusted for era; this is better than average for the average NBA player but not all that good for someone shooting as much as Kobe) OBSERVATIONS FROM THE COMMENTS Kenn: I think his averages in elimination games are also pretty bad considering how people say he was clutch. He averages 22 ppg on 41% field goal percentage, 28% from three and 77% from the free throw line. All down trends from his typical playoff averages, where as other players like Jordan stepped up their play even. Xitong Zou: If Kobe was the GOAT, he wouldn’t have blown a 3–1 lead to Nash’s Suns in the middle of his prime in 2006. Kobe fans make so many excuses for this. He had Lamar Odom on his team who was outplaying Marion in the series. Stoudemire was out. Leandro Barbosa outscored him in the Game 7. It’s really inexcusable, but this bad choke is completely forgotten by NBA fans. REFERENCES AND LINKS StatMuse Basketball Reference The aforementioned D-RAPM analysis and comments: #NBA #KOBE #MRB-NBA #MRB-KOBE #MBNBA #MRBKOBE 403 views on 7–6–2024

Name: Mike Burch
Question: What is a poem on the moon in any specific language?
Answer: MOON POEMS by Michael R. Burch These are poems about the moon and moonlight from various languages including Chinese, English, French, German, Indonesian, Japanese, Kurdish, Latin, Native American, Persian, Spanish, Tamil, Turkish, Ukrainian and Urdu. Quiet Night Thoughts by Li Bai aka Li Po loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Moonlight illuminates my bed as frost brightens the ground. Lifting my eyes, the moon allures. Lowering my eyes, I long for home. My interpretation of this famous poem is a bit different from the norm. The moon symbolizes love, so I imagine the moon shining on Li Bai’s bed to be suggestive, an invitation. A man might lower his eyes to avoid seeing something his wife would not approve of. This world? Moonlit dew flicked from a crane’s bill. —Eihei Dogen Kigen, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Outside my window the plums, blossoming, within their curled buds, contain the spring; the moon is reflected in the cup-like whorls of the lovely flowers I gather and twirl. —Eihei Dogen Kigen, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch The moon has long since set; the Pleiades are gone; now half the night is spent yet here I sleep alone. —Sappho, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Kin by Michael R. Burch O pale, austere moon, haughty beauty ... what do we know of love, or duty? …“The sun and lady-moon, they lave their tresses in the main, and find such cleansing in each wave, they return twice bright again.”… —excerpt from “The Fisher” by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Pausing between clouds the moon rests in the eyes of its beholders —Matsuo Basho, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Tzu Yeh (circa 400 BC) loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch I could not sleep with the full moon haunting my bed! I thought I heard―here, there, everywhere― disembodied voices calling my name! Helplessly I cried "Yes!" to the phantom air! Excerpt from “To the Moon” by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe loose translations/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Scattered, pole to starry pole, glide Cynthia's mild beams, whispering to the receptive soul whatever moonbeams mean. Bathing valley, hill and dale with her softening light, loosening from earth’s frigid chains my restless heart tonight! Over the landscape, near and far, broods darkly glowering night; yet welcoming as Friendship’s eye, she, soft!, bequeaths her light. Touched in turn by joy and pain, my startled heart responds, then floats, as Whimsy paints each scene, to soar with her, beyond... I mean Whimsy in the sense of both the Romantic Imagination and caprice. Here, I have the idea of Peter Pan flying off with Tinker Bell to Neverland. I think of you when the sun shines softly on me; also when the moon silvers each tree. —excerpt from “Near His Beloved” by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Moon Poem by Michael R. Burch I climb the mountain to inquire of the moon … the advantages of loftiness, absence, distance. Is it true that it feels no pain, or will she contradict me? Originally published by Borderless Journal (Singapore). The use of "it" and "she" is intentional, because the speaker doesn't know if the moon is impervious to pain or has consciousness. By such pale moonlight even the wisteria's fragrance seems distant. —Yosa Buson, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Leaves like crows’ shadows flirt with a lonely moon. —Kaga no Chiyo, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch In this Ordinary Swoon by Michael R. Burch In this ordinary swoon as I pass from life to death, I feel no heat from the cold, pale moon; I feel no sympathy for breath. Who I am and why I came, I do not know; nor does it matter. The end of every man’s the same and every god’s as mad as a hatter. I do not fear the letting go; I only fear the clinging on to hope when there’s no hope, although I lift my face to the blazing sun and feel the greater intensity of the wilder inferno within me. You left our house as the moon deserts night's skies, as the evening light abandons its cycle. —Mirza Ghalib, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Before you judge a man for his sins be sure to trudge many moons in his moccasins. —Native American proverb, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Oh, brilliant moon is it true that even you must fly as if you're tardy? ―Issa, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch The moon has risen once again, yet you are not here. My heart is a blazing pyre; what do I do? —Majrooh Sultanpuri, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Dispensing Keys by Hafiz aka Hafez loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch The imbecile constructs cages for everyone he knows, while the sage (who has to duck his head whenever the moon glows) keeps dispensing keys all night long to the beautiful, rowdy, prison gang. The Lonely Earth by Kajal Ahmad loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch The pale celestial bodies never bid her "Good morning!" nor do the creative stars kiss her. Earth, where so many tender persuasions and roses lie interred, might expire for the lack of a glance, or an odor. She's a lonely dusty orb, so very lonely!, as she observes the moon's patchwork attire knowing the sun's an imposter who sears with rays he has stolen for himself and who looks down on the moon and earth like lodgers. To the boy Elis by Georg Trakl, an Austrian poet who wrote in German loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Elis, when the blackbird cries from the black forest, it announces your downfall. Your lips sip the rock-spring's blue coolness. Your brow sweats blood recalling ancient myths and dark interpretations of birds' flight. Yet you enter the night with soft footfalls; the ripe purple grapes hang suspended as you wave your arms more beautifully in the blueness. A thornbush crackles; where now are your moonlike eyes? How long, oh Elis, have you been dead? A monk dips waxed fingers into your body's hyacinth; Our silence is a black abyss from which sometimes a docile animal emerges slowly lowering its heavy lids. A black dew drips from your temples: the lost gold of vanished stars. TRANSLATOR'S NOTE: I believe that in the second stanza the blood on Elis's forehead may be a reference to the apprehensive bloody sweat of Jesus in the garden of Gethsemane. If my interpretation is correct, Elis hears the blackbird's cries, anticipates the danger represented by a harbinger of death, but elects to continue rather than turn back. From what I have been able to gather, the color blue had a special significance for Georg Trakl: it symbolized longing and perhaps a longing for death. The colors blue, purple and black may represent a progression toward death in the poem. Full Moon by Yahya Kemal Beyatli loose translation by Nurgül Yayman and Michael R. Burch You are so lovely the full moon just might delight in your rising, as curious and bright, to vanquish night. But what can a mortal man do, dear, but hope? I’ll ponder your mysteries and (hmmmm) try to cope. We both know you have every right to say no. Canción del jinete (“The Horseman’s Song” or “Song of the Rider”) by Federico Garcia Lorca loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Cordoba. Distant and lone. Black pony, big moon, olives in my saddlebag. Although my pony knows the way, I never will reach Cordoba. High plains, high winds. Black pony, blood moon. Death awaits me, watching from the towers of Cordoba. Such a long, long way! Oh my brave pony! Death awaits me before I arrive in Cordoba! Cordoba. Distant and lone. Gacela of the Dark Death by Federico Garcia Lorca loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch I want to sleep the dreamless sleep of apples far from the bustle of cemeteries. I want to sleep the dream-filled sleep of the child who longed to cut out his heart on the high seas. I don't want to hear how the corpse retains its blood, or how the putrefying mouth continues accumulating water. I don't want to be informed of the grasses’ torture sessions, nor of the moon with its serpent's snout scuttling until dawn… Kindred by Michael R. Burch Rise, pale disastrous moon! What is love, but a heightened effect of time, light and distance? Did you burn once, before you became so remote, so detached, so coldly, inhumanly lustrous, before you were able to assume the very pallor of love itself? What is the dawn now, to you or to me? We are as one, out of favor with the sun. We would exhume the white corpse of love for a last dance, and yet we will not. We will let her be, let her abide, for she is nothing now, to you or to me. If the Last Rom Dies by Mixa Kozimirenko loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch If the last Rom dies, a star would vanish above the tent, mountains and valleys moan, horses whinny in open fields, thunderclouds shroud the moon, fiddles and guitars gently weep, giants and dwarfs mourn… Song by Renée Vivien loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch When the moon weeps, illuminating flowers on the graves of the faithful, my memories creep back to you, wrapped in flightless wings. It's getting late; soon we will sleep (your eyes already half closed) steeped in the shimmering air. O, the agony of burning roses: your forehead discloses a heavy despondency, though your hair floats lightly ... In the night sky the stars burn whitely as the Goddess nightly resurrects flowers that fear the sun and die before dawn ... Undine by Renée Vivien loose translation/interpretation by Kim Cherub (an alias of Michael R. Burch) Your laughter startles, your caresses rake. Your cold kisses love the evil they do. Your eyes—blue lotuses drifting on a lake. Lilies are less pallid than your face. You move like water parting. Your hair falls in rootlike tangles. Your words like treacherous rapids rise. Your arms, flexible as reeds, strangle, Choking me like tubular river reeds. I shiver in their enlacing embrace. Drowning without an illuminating moon, I vanish without a trace, lost in a nightly swoon. "Vande Mataram" by Subramanya Bharathi, a Tamil poet loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch …Your skies are moonlit through the nightwatch’s hours while your groves emit the soft incense of flowers. Birds chirping in the trees remind us of your blessings. Venerably, we bow before you… Ehad-e-Tifli (“The Age of Infancy”) by Allama Iqbal aka Muhammad Iqbal loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch The earth and the heavens remained unknown to me, My mother's bosom was my only world. Her embraces communicated life's joys While I babbled meaningless sounds. During my infancy if someone alarmed me The clank of the door chain consoled me. At night I observed the moon, Following its flight through distant clouds. By day I pondered earth’s terrain Only to be surprised by convenient explanations. My eyes ingested light, my lips sought speech, I was curiosity incarnate. Catullus VII aka Carmina 7: “How Many Kisses” loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch You ask, Lesbia, how many kisses are enough, or more than enough, to satisfy me? As many as the Libyan sands swirling in incense-bearing Cyrene between the torrid oracle of Jove and the sacred tomb of Battiades. Or as many as the stars observing amorous men making love furtively on a moonless night. As many of your kisses are enough, and more than enough, for mad Catullus, as long as there are too many to be counted by inquisitors and by malicious-tongued bewitchers. THE WORLD'S FIRST FACE by W. S. Rendra loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Illuminated by the pale moonlight the groom carries his bride up the hill— both of them naked, both consisting of nothing but themselves… …Illuminated by the pale moonlight the groom carries his bride up the hill— both of them naked, to recreate the world's first face. If You Forget Me by Pablo Neruda loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch I need you to know one thing ... You know how it goes: if I gaze up at the glowing moon, if observe the blazing autumn's reddening branches from my window, if I touch the impalpable ash of the charred log's wrinkled body ... everything returns me to you, as if everything that exists —all aromas, sights, solids— were small boats sailing toward those isles of yours that await me… These are original poems of mine about the moon… Distances by Michael R. Burch Moonbeams on water — the reflected light of a halcyon star now drowning in night… So your memories are. Footprints on beaches now flooding with water; the small, broken ribcage of some primitive slaughter… So near, yet so far. Goddess by Michael R. Burch “What will you conceive in me?”— I asked her. But she only smiled. “Naked, I bore your child when the wolf wind howled, when the cold moon scowled . . . naked, and gladly.” “What will become of me?”— I asked her, as she absently stroked my hand. Centuries later, I understand; she whispered—“I Am.” This was the first poem to appear in the first issue of Romantics Quarterly; it has also been published by Penny Dreadful, Unlikely Stories, Underground Poets, Poetically Speaking, Poetry Life & Times and Little Brown Poetry Adrift by Michael R. Burch I helplessly loved you although I was lost in the veils of your eyes, grown blind to the cost of my ignorant folly —your unreadable rune— as leashed tides obey an indecipherable moon. Free Fall by Michael R. Burch These cloudless nights, the sky becomes a wheel where suns revolve around an axle star … Look there, and choose. Decide which moon is yours. Sink Lethe-ward, held only by a heel. Advantage. Disadvantage. Who can tell? To see is not to know, but you can feel the tug sometimes—the gravity, the shell as lustrous as damp pearl. You sink, you reel toward some draining revelation. Air— too thin to grasp, to breathe. Such pressure. Gasp. The stars invert, electric, everywhere. And so we fall, down-tumbling through night’s fissure … two beings pale, intent to fall forever around each other—fumbling at love’s tether … now separate, now distant, now together. Sunset by Michael R. Burch This poem is dedicated to my grandfather, George Edwin Hurt, who died April 4, 1998. Between the prophecies of morning and twilight’s revelations of wonder, the sky is ripped asunder. The moon lurks in the clouds, waiting, as if to plunder the dusk of its lilac iridescence, and in the bright-tentacled sunset we imagine a presence full of the fury of lost innocence. What we find within strange whorls of drifting flame, brief patterns mauling winds deform and maim, we recognize at once, but cannot name. Heat Lightening by Michael R. Burch Each night beneath the elms, we never knew which lights beyond dark hills might stall, advance, then lurch into strange headbeams tilted up like searchlights seeking contact in the distance … Quiescent unions … thoughts of bliss, of hope … long-dreamt appearances of wished-on stars … like childhood’s long-occluded, nebulous slow drift of half-formed visions … slip and bra … Wan moonlight traced your features, perilous, in danger of extinction, should your hair fall softly on my eyes, or should a kiss cause them to close, or should my fingers dare to leave off childhood for some new design of whiter lace, of flesh incarnadine. Instruction by Michael R. Burch Toss this poem aside to the filigreed and the prettified tide of sunset. Strike my name, and still it is all the same. The onset of night is in the despairing skies; each hut shuts its bright bewildered eyes. The wind sighs and my heart sighs with her— my only companion, O Lovely Drifter! Still, men are not wise. The moon appears; the arms of the wind lift her, pooling the light of her silver portent, while men, impatient, are beings of hurried and harried despair. Now willows entangle their fragrant hair. Men sleep. Cornsilk tassels the moonbright air. Deep is the sea; the stars are fair. I reap. Moon Lake by Michael R. Burch Starlit recorder of summer nights, what magic spell bewitches you? They say that all lovers love first in the dark … Is it true? Is it true? Is it true? Starry-eyed seer of all that appears and all that has appeared— What sights have you seen? What dreams have you dreamed? What rhetoric have you heard? Is love an oration, or is it a word? Have you heard? Have you heard? Have you heard? I believe I wrote this poem around age 18, during my "Romantic Period." Infinity by Michael R. Burch Have you tasted the bitterness of tears of despair? Have you watched the sun sink through such pale, balmless air that your heart sought its shell like a crab on a beach, then scuttled inside to be safe, out of reach? Might I lift you tonight from earth’s wreckage and damage on these waves gently rising to pay the moon homage? Or better, perhaps, let me say that I, too, have dreamed of infinity … windswept and blue. This is one of the first poems that made me feel like a "real" poet. I remember reading the poem and asking myself, "Did I really write that?" Many years later, I'm still glad that I wrote it, and it still makes me feel like a real poet! This is another poem that was longer and got "pared down" to its best lines. I believe I wrote it around 1976, at age 18. She Was Very Strange, and Beautiful by Michael R. Burch She was very strange, and beautiful, like a violet mist enshrouding hills before night falls when the hoot owl calls and the cricket trills and the envapored moon hangs low and full. She was very strange, in a pleasant way, as the hummingbird flies madly still, so I drank my fill of her every word. What she knew of love, she demurred to say. She was meant to leave, as the wind must blow, as the sun must set, as the rain must fall. Though she gave her all, I had nothing left … yet I smiled, bereft, in her receding glow. To Flower by Michael R. Burch When Pentheus ["grief'] went into the mountains in the garb of the baccae, his mother [Agave] and the other maenads, possessed by Dionysus, tore him apart (Euripides, Bacchae; Apollodorus 3.5.2; Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.511-733; Hyginus, Fabulae 184). The agave dies as soon as it blooms; the moonflower, or night-blooming cereus, is a desert plant of similar fate. We are not long for this earth, I know— you and I, all our petals incurled, till a night of pale brilliance, moonflower aglow. Is there love anywhere in this strange world? The Agave knows best when it's time to die and rages to life with such rapturous leaves her name means Illustrious. Each hour more high, she claws toward heaven, for, if she believes in love at all, she has left it behind to flower, to flower. When darkness falls she wilts down to meet it, where something crawls: beheaded, bewildered. And since love is blind, she never adored it, nor watches it go. Can we be as she is, moonflower aglow? In Praise of Meter by Michael R. Burch The earth is full of rhythms so precise the octave of the crystal can produce a trillion oscillations, yet not lose a second's beat. The ear needs no device to hear the unsprung rhythms of the couch drown out the mouth's; the lips can be debauched by kisses, should the heart put back its watch and find the pulse of love, and sing, devout. If moons and tides in interlocking dance obey their numbers, what's been left to chance? Should poets be more lax—their circumstance as humble as it is?—or readers wince to see their ragged numbers thin, to hear the moans of drones drown out the Chanticleer? Originally published by The Eclectic Muse, then by The Best of the Eclectic Muse 1989-2003 Finally to Burn (the Fall and Resurrection of Icarus) by Michael R. Burch Athena takes me sometimes by the hand and we go levitating through strange Dreamlands where Apollo sleeps in his dark forgetting and Passion seems like a wise bloodletting and all I remember ,upon awaking, is: to Love sometimes is like forsaking one’s Being—to glide heroically beyond thought, forsaking the here for the There and the Not. * O, finally to Burn, gravity beyond escaping! To plummet is Bliss when the blisters breaking rain down red scabs on the earth’s mudpuddle ... Feathers and wax and the watchers huddle ... Flocculent sheep, O, and innocent lambs!, I will rock me to sleep on the waves’ iambs. * To sleep's sweet relief from Love’s exhausting Dream, for the Night has Wings gentler than Moonbeams— they will flit me to Life like a huge-eyed Phoenix fluttering off to quarry the Sphinx. * Riddlemethis, riddlemethat, Rynosseross, throw out the Welcome Mat. Quixotic, I seek Love amid the tarnished rusted-out steel when to live is varnish. To Dream—that’s the thing! Aye, that Genie I’ll rub, soak by the candle, aflame in the tub. * Riddlemethis, riddlemethat, Rynosseross, throw out the Welcome Mat. Somewhither, somewhither aglitter and strange, we must moult off all knowledge or perish caged. * I am reconciled to Life somewhere beyond thought— I’ll Live the Elsewhere, I’ll Dream of the Naught. Methinks it no journey; to tarry’s a waste, so fatten the oxen; make a nice baste. I’m coming, Fool Tom, we have Somewhere to Go, though we injure noone, ourselves wildaglow. A final stereo fades into silence and now there is seldom a murmur to trouble the slumber of these ancient halls. I stand by a window where others have watched the passage of time—alone, not untouched. And I am as they were . . . unsure . . . for the days stretch out ahead, a bewildering maze. II. Ah, faithless lover— that I had never touched your breast, nor felt the stirrings of my heart, which until that moment had peacefully slept. For now I have known the exhilaration of a heart that has vaulted the Pinnacle of Love, and the result of each such infatuation— the long freefall to earth, as the moon glides above. III. A solitary clock chimes the hour from far above the campus, but my peers, returning from their dances, heed it not. IV. Ungentle maiden— when Time has etched His little lines so carelessly across your brow, perhaps I will love you less than now. And when cruel Time has stolen your youth, as He certainly shall in course, perhaps you will wish you had taken me along with my broken heart, even as He will take you with yours. V. A measureless rhythm rules the night— few have heard it, but I have shared it, and its secret is mine. To put it into words is as to extract the sweetness from honey and must be done as gently as a butterfly cleans its wings. But when it is captured, it is gone again; its usefulness is only that it lulls to sleep. VI. So sleep, my love, to the cadence of night, to the moans of the moonlit hills' bass chorus of frogs, while the deep valleys fill with the nightjar’s shrill, cryptic trills. But I will not sleep this night, nor any . . . how can I—when my dreams are always of your perfect face ringed by soft whorls of fretted lace, framed by your perfect pillowcase? VII. If I had been born when knights roamed the earth and mad kings ruled savage lands, I might have turned to the ministry, to the solitude of a monastery. But there are no monks or hermits today— theirs is a lost occupation carried on, if at all, merely for sake of tradition. For today man abhors solitude— he craves companions, song and drink, seldom seeking a quiet moment, to sit alone, by himself, to think. VIII. And so I cannot shut myself off from the rest of the world, to spend my days in philosophy and my nights in tears of self-sympathy. No, I must continue as best I can, and learn to keep my thoughts away from those glorious, uproarious moments of youth, centuries past though lost but a day. IX. Yes, I must discipline myself and adjust to these lackluster days when men display no chivalry and romance is the "old-fashioned" way. X. A single stereo flares into song and the first faint light of morning has pierced the sky's black awning once again. XI. This is a sacred place, for those who leave, leave better than they came. But those who stay, while they are here, add, with their sleepless nights and tears, quaint sprigs of ivy to the walls of these hallowed halls. I vividly remember writing the first version of “These Hallowed Halls” early my freshman year of college as I watched my peers returning from rush week parties by the light of an eerie moon.

Question: Which do you believe is true, creationism or evolutionism?
Answer: EVOLUTION VS. CREATIONISM by Michael R. Burch Evolution is a real thing, proven by the fossil record and the science of genetics. Human DNA is very similar to that of our closest relatives among the animals, the great apes. Genes confirm what our eyes tell us: that we are closer to the great apes than to any other animals on the planet we share. Furthermore, we can see evolution happening before our eyes. For instance, when coal-fueled power plants in England started spewing black soot into the air, butterflies that had once been brightly colored soon turned black. We can also see microscopic organisms like the coronavirus mutating at incredible rates, faster than scientists can keep up with them. It seem likely that the “great leap” in human consciousness that took place around 10,000 years ago was the result of some sort of mutation in human brains. Creationism is a fantasy-like belief without any support. Which doesn’t mean some sort of creator or creators don’t exist, just that there is no reason to believe anything in particular about them. While it seems impossible to prove or disprove the existence of a creator or creators, what we do know, without a doubt, is that the biblical account of creation is ancient hogwash, for the following reasons, among many others: When people argue for creationism here on Quora, they usually mean biblical creationism, which is pure hogwash. As for the other sort of creationism, with some mysterious entity about whom we know absolutely nothing creating the universe for unknowable reasons, where does such a belief get us? Such beliefs not only seem illogical, they have no benefit outside entertainment in science fiction and fairy tales. There is, I believe, a valid question about how something as complex as the human eyeball or the human reproductive system could have evolved at random. But the solution doesn’t require “gods.” For instance, genes could have acquired intelligence.
